outbreaks.title: Ebola (Bundibugyo virus) — DRC, with spread to Kenya and Nigeria
outbreaks.status: PHEIC · Active — 10,000+ confirmed cases in DRC; Kenya cluster (9 cases) and first Nigeria case (20 Oct)
outbreaks.desc: As of data to 25 October 2026 (ECDC, published 27 October), DRC has 10,060 confirmed cases and 4,887 deaths, with 2,684 recovered and 1,008 patients in isolation, across 8 provinces and 66 of 178 health zones. By province (cases/deaths): Ituri 7,211/3,370; North Kivu 2,309/1,293; Haut-Uélé 436/190; Tshopo 83/27; Bas-Uélé 13/4; South Kivu 3/1; Nord-Ubangi 3/1; Sud-Ubangi 2/1. WHO's DON-622 (23 October, data to 20 October: 9,704 cases, 4,687 deaths, crude CFR 48.3%) counted 976 new cases and 482 deaths since 8 October — 307 of those deaths in the community rather than in treatment centres — and contact follow-up at 79.7% of 30,130 contacts, well below the 95% target. UKHSA notes new cases in Ituri are falling, while North Kivu (the highest provincial CFR, 55.9%) keeps rising; the newest affected zone, Wapinda in Nord-Ubangi, borders the Central African Republic. This is the largest Bundibugyo outbreak on record and the second-largest Ebola outbreak of any species. The PHEIC (17 May) remains in force. WHO's formal risk assessment (very high in DRC, high in bordering countries, low globally) dates from 14 August and a revision is under way.
outbreaks.more: KENYA: 9 confirmed cases, all in one cluster linked to the imported index case (a Kenyan who had lived in DRC, travelled by road to Kampala and flew to Nairobi on 3 October; died 5 October). The 8 secondary cases are 4 family members and 4 health and care workers who treated him. ECDC records 2 deaths (the second on 23 October) and the last case reported on 20 October. All 135 contacts were traced and quarantined; the first 20 finished 21-day follow-up on 25–26 October, with 98 still monitored. The Health Ministry reports no community transmission and says the end of the outbreak is 'within reach'. NIGERIA — first case in over a decade: a 42-year-old Swiss woman, wife of a Swiss embassy staff member in Abuja, confirmed 20 October (onset 7 October, sought care 11 October). She had travelled in Uganda and, per the Swiss government, not in DRC; the source of exposure is still under investigation, and how a Uganda exposure fits the dates has not been explained publicly. NCDC lists 53 primary contacts, most of them health workers; a suspected case in Rivers State tested negative. She was evacuated to Switzerland with a close contact on 26 October. The 13-day gap between arrival (3 October) and diagnosis is the main concern. UGANDA: its earlier outbreak (20 cases, 2 deaths) was declared over on 27 August; 60 contacts of the Kenyan case completed follow-up there. EUROPE: there have been 5 imported or medevac cases since May (Germany ×2, France, UK, Netherlands), plus the 26 October Swiss evacuation; ECDC rates the risk to the EU/EEA population as very low. COUNTERMEASURES: no Bundibugyo vaccine or treatment is licensed. The TUMAINI Phase 2/3 trial of several vaccine candidates, including Ervebo, enrolled its first participants in Bunia on 23 October. The Ervebo frontline-worker campaign in Kisangani (since 27 August) continues, but WHO says it is not known whether Ervebo protects against Bundibugyo in humans. Confirmed counts likely understate the true scale given the community deaths, conflict and gaps in follow-up.
outbreaks.src: ECDC Ebola (Bundibugyo) event update, 27 Oct 2026 (data to 25–26 Oct); WHO DON-622, 23 Oct 2026; UKHSA Outbreaks under monitoring week 42 (to 20 Oct 2026); Citizen Digital (Kenya MoH), 22 Oct 2026; Africanews/AFP (Nigeria evacuation, 53 contacts), 26 Oct 2026; Malay Mail/AFP (Swiss statement), 24 Oct 2026

outbreaks.title: Measles Outbreak — Bangladesh
outbreaks.status: Active — world's largest current measles outbreak (per CDC)
outbreaks.desc: As of 8 am on 26 October 2026, Bangladesh's DGHS reports 222,552 suspected and 23,478 laboratory-confirmed measles cases in 2026, and 1,233 deaths (1,129 among suspected and 104 among confirmed cases). In the latest 24 hours there were 1,388 new suspected cases, 78 newly confirmed cases and 6 child deaths, so transmission is still running at well over 1,000 suspected cases a day. Deaths have risen from 1,009 on 10 September and about 1,096 on 27 September — roughly 140 more in a month. Hospitals have recorded 197,999 suspected-measles admissions since 15 March. It is Bangladesh's deadliest measles outbreak in decades (the country recorded 132 cases and no deaths in all of 2025), and CDC lists it as the world's largest current measles outbreak.
outbreaks.more: Vaccination: the emergency measles-rubella campaign that began on 5 April reached roughly 18–19.75 million children against an 18 million target, but about four million were missed and DGHS has acknowledged that herd immunity was not achieved. A follow-up campaign had been announced as being prepared, but no start date was located. WHO and UNICEF link the crisis to immunization gaps in 2024–2025 after the political upheaval; the Health Minister told parliament in September that procurement-policy changes in that period caused a vaccine shortage. Chronic child malnutrition is raising case fatality. 79% of early cases were in children under five (WHO DON-598). Media death tallies of 1,240 or more after 26 October come from later daily DGHS bulletins.
outbreaks.src: The Business Standard (relaying DGHS bulletin to 8 am, 26 Oct 2026); IANS, 26 Oct 2026; Dhaka Tribune daily DGHS reports, Oct 2026; Business Standard via Wikipedia (10 Sep 2026 totals); WHO DON-598 (Apr 2026)

outbreaks.title: First Documented Human Shamonda Virus Infection — Fatal Case, Lyon (France)
outbreaks.status: Single case — no onward transmission; authorities report no general-population risk
outbreaks.desc: On 22 October 2026 France reported the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus, an orthobunyavirus (Simbu serogroup) that infects cattle and is spread by Culicoides biting midges. The patient was severely immunocompromised, was being treated in Lyon and died in early October. The leading hypothesis is infection in eastern France, where the virus circulated among animals in spring and summer 2026. The Ministry of Agriculture says there is no identifiable risk to the general population, and the Health Ministry called the death an 'exceptional event' probably explained by the patient's underlying condition. ECDC opened a public-health event on 27 October.
outbreaks.more: Why it is tracked: it is a first-ever spillover of an animal arbovirus into a human, found in a European clinical setting. That is the kind of novel zoonotic signal that genomic diagnostics are now picking up in immunocompromised patients, and it comes as Culicoides-borne livestock viruses (bluetongue, Schmallenberg — a close Simbu-group relative — and now Shamonda) are expanding north in Europe with climate change. How it was detected was not described in the sources located.
outbreaks.src: Al Jazeera/Reuters, 22 Oct 2026; The Wire/AP, 22 Oct 2026; ECDC public health events listing ('First detection of Shamonda virus in an immunocompromised patient, France'), 27 Oct 2026

outbreaks.title: Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute — Technician Death, Suspected Lab Exposure (Russia)
outbreaks.status: Unexplained — cause of death undetermined; WHO says a lab-associated exposure 'cannot be fully excluded'
outbreaks.desc: A 28-year-old technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was hospitalised on 29 September and died on 1–2 October. Local media citing anonymous sources reported a broken tube of Yersinia pestis on 25 September. Russia denies this: authorities classify the death as 'pneumonia of undetermined etiology', say plague was not the cause, and report that two independent investigations found no laboratory biosafety or biosecurity incident. WHO's DON-620 (10 October) reports that the patient and contacts were tested for a broad pathogen panel, including plague, with all high-threat pathogen tests negative (more than 5,500 tests across five Rospotrebnadzor institutions); that all contacts stayed asymptomatic; and that monitoring ended by 8–9 October, when the governor lifted the hospital quarantine. WHO adds that its confidence is limited because the cause of death is still unknown. Since the worker handled high-consequence pathogens, WHO says 'a laboratory-associated exposure cannot be fully excluded', and it has recommended further testing of clinical specimens at reference laboratories.
outbreaks.more: Contacts: about 197 identified. The only infections found among them were COVID-19 (2), rhinovirus (2–3), one Haemophilus case and other opportunistic infections. Officially, quarantine applied only to the Shelekhov District Hospital inpatient unit; media reports of wider hospital closures and a 'second case' were denied by the authorities, who called a circulating plague-quarantine 'resolution' fake (13 October). Hong Kong and Macau added health declarations and checks for travellers from Irkutsk Oblast (12 October). ECDC said on 16 October that the information was still not enough for a firm conclusion. Unverified social-media claims of further deaths (19–20 October) have not been confirmed by any authority. The institute's 18th CIS plague conference, planned for Irkutsk on 21–22 October, was moved to 11–12 November 2026 under a Rospotrebnadzor order of 21 October; no reason was given (per the institute and conference websites, as compiled by PlagueIntel). Assessment: there is no evidence of onward transmission. As a biosafety question the event remains OPEN — no pathogen has been named, no lab results have been published, and WHO has not independently verified the findings. There is no public evidence linking it to any weapons activity.
outbreaks.src: WHO DON-620, 10 Oct 2026; Al Jazeera, 10 Oct 2026; UN News, Oct 2026; CNN, 7 Oct 2026; PlagueIntel Irkutsk timeline (status as of 26 Oct 2026; secondary compilation); ECDC CDTR (16 Oct 2026)

outbreaks.title: Avian & Zoonotic Influenza at the Human–Animal Interface — WHO Monthly Summary
outbreaks.desc: New US human H5N1 case: on 15 October 2026 Yakima County (Washington State) reported a confirmed case in a worker exposed to infected dairy cattle. The case was mild, not hospitalised and isolating at home, and contacts are being monitored. That brings the US total since April 2024 to 72 cases in 13 states (one death): 42 from dairy cattle, 24 from poultry farms and culling, 3 from other animals and 3 with unknown exposure (ECDC, 19 October). It is Washington's first dairy-linked case; its 12 earlier cases were linked to poultry (11) or other animals (1). Globally, WHO's Western Pacific Region counts 1,003 human H5N1 cases and 479 deaths (CFR 47.8%) in 25 countries from 2003 to 6 September 2026. There is still no sustained human-to-human transmission, and WHO, CDC and ECDC rate the risk to the general population as low (CDC rates it moderate to high for people with exposure to infected animals).
outbreaks.more: Cambodia: 6 human H5N1 cases in 2026; the latest, a 49-year-old poultry farmer in Oddar Meanchey, was reported on 28 September (Cambodia had 18 cases and 9 deaths in 2025). China reports sporadic H9N2 infections, mostly mild and in children; the latest had onset on 7 September in Guangdong, and ECDC updated its H9N2 overview on 26 October. The latest H5N6 case had onset on 16 April (Chongqing). WHO's 6 September human–animal interface summary recorded 1 H5N1, 3 H9N2 and 2 swine-variant H1N2 cases for 8 August–6 September. H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b continues to circulate in wild birds, poultry and US dairy cattle. Genotype B3.13, found in US cattle, has not been detected in Europe, and the EU/EEA has no confirmed human H5N1 cases.
outbreaks.src: ECDC Avian influenza A(H5N1) human cases, United States, update 19 Oct 2026; UKHSA Outbreaks under monitoring week 42 (15 Oct 2026); WHO WPRO Avian Influenza Weekly Update No. 1064 (2 Oct 2026); WHO human–animal interface summary, 6 Sep 2026; The Star (Malaysia), 28 Sep 2026

outbreaks.title: Broader Transmission of Mpox (Clade Ib MPXV) — Global Situation
outbreaks.status: Active — PHEIC lifted 5 Sep 2025; sustained transmission continues
outbreaks.desc: WHO's 69th mpox situation report (14 September 2026) counts 52,424 laboratory-confirmed cases and 238 deaths (CFR 0.5%) across 35 African countries between 1 January 2025 and 16 August 2026; in the latest six-week window (6 Jul–16 Aug) 11 African countries had active transmission, with 1,153 confirmed cases and 7 deaths. WHO lifted the mpox PHEIC on 5 September 2025 but continues to advise emergency preparedness, and clade Ib has since caused locally acquired cases in countries across four of six WHO regions.
outbreaks.more: South Africa: 26 laboratory-confirmed cases since 1 January as of 18 October (up from 22 on 22 September). These comprise Western Cape 18 (16 locally acquired, 2 imported), Gauteng 3, Eastern Cape 2, Free State 2 and KwaZulu-Natal 1. Clade was known for 17 cases: 13 clade Ib and 4 clade IIb. 25 of 26 cases are male (median age 37). Madagascar has had the largest clade Ib outbreak to date (1,092 confirmed cases and 3 deaths by 19 April 2026). Singapore reported its first clade Ib cases on 2 April 2026, and Estonia its first clade I case in August 2026. UK: UKHSA's 8 October overview (data to 30 September) records 226 clade Ib cases since 2023 against 972 clade IIb, with clade Ib cases exceeding clade IIb from July 2026. A recombinant Ib/IIb virus was identified in a traveller in England in October 2025. As of late October, no WHO situation report newer than #69 (14 September) was located.
outbreaks.src: WHO mpox external situation report #69 (14 Sep 2026); TimesLIVE/South African Health Dept, 18 Oct 2026; WHO situation report #65 (Apr 2026); WHO DON-587; UKHSA Mpox outbreak epidemiological overview, 8 Oct 2026

outbreaks.title: MERS-CoV — Global Update
outbreaks.desc: WHO data reported by UKHSA (15 October 2026) record 8 laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV cases, including 1 death, in Saudi Arabia from 1 January to 5 October 2026. The cases were spread across Al Jouf, Arar, Hafr Al-Batin, Riyadh (2), Tabuk and Taif (2). Two reported direct camel contact and six did not; none were linked to each other, and there were no health-worker infections, so WHO treats them as sporadic zoonotic spillover. The global total since 2012 is 2,643 cases and 965 deaths (Saudi Arabia 2,232 and 870). ECDC's own series, last updated 19 October, still described 2026 as the lowest surveillance-detected level since 2014; its earlier count of two 2026 cases reflects reporting lags. ECDC assesses the risk to the EU/EEA as low.
outbreaks.more: For context, 2025 saw 19 cases and 4 deaths globally, including two travel-associated cases in France. The UK has had 5 imported or related cases (2 deaths) since 2012, the last in 2018.
outbreaks.src: UKHSA Outbreaks under monitoring week 42 (15 Oct 2026, citing WHO); ECDC MERS-CoV monthly update (19 Oct 2026); ECDC MERS-CoV worldwide overview (5 Oct 2026); WHO DON-591 (Dec 2025)

outbreaks.title: Cholera — West and Central Africa (Multi-country)
outbreaks.desc: ECDC's latest monthly overview (as of 28 September 2026) counts 249,136 cholera cases and 1,970 deaths worldwide since 1 January 2026 — about 43% fewer cases and 56% fewer deaths than the same point in 2025 (436,268 cases and 4,449 deaths). In the latest period (26 Aug–28 Sep) 46,153 new cases and 140 new deaths were reported, against 42,717 cases and 257 deaths in the previous period (plus 2,080 reported retrospectively). The largest contributors were Afghanistan (34,378 cases, 10 deaths), DRC (8,505 cases, the most deaths at 107), Yemen (1,885), Angola (748) and Congo (299). Nigeria, which dominated the August update, is no longer among the top five for the latest period, which suggests part of that August figure was backlog reporting. Country figures use different reporting cut-off dates.
outbreaks.more: Regional detail from UNICEF/WHO (12 Aug): cholera was active across six countries in two corridors — the Lake Chad Basin (Chad, Cameroon, Nigeria) and the Congo River Basin (DRC, Republic of Congo, CAR). Seasonal rains, flooding, displacement and cross-border movement accelerate spread; children are disproportionately affected. In DRC, cholera is occurring alongside the Ebola emergency in the east and the DRC death toll (107 in the latest period) is the highest of any country. UNICEF sought $15 million to scale up its six-month response. ECDC published a further monthly update on 27 October 2026, but it could not be accessed for this refresh, so the 28 September figures above remain the latest verified.
outbreaks.src: ECDC Cholera Worldwide Overview (28 Sep 2026); UNICEF/UN News, 12 Aug 2026

outbreaks.title: H1N1 (Seasonal Influenza) — Delhi, India
outbreaks.desc: Delhi's 2026 H1N1 season has been far larger than usual. Delhi Health Department data put cases at 1,777 on 20 August, 2,308 by 25 August (when ICMR said this was roughly six to eight times a normal year) and 3,218 by 31 August. ICMR also recorded about 650 cases of other influenza variants. H1N1 has displaced H3N2 as the dominant subtype, circulating with influenza B and COVID-19. ICMR (Director-General Rajiv Bahl) says the virus is not a new or more virulent strain and matches the Northern Hemisphere vaccine strains. Most infections have been mild, with no ICU or ventilator cases reported as of late August. (This replaces this tracker's earlier 'plateau' reading, which was based on a stale cumulative figure.)
outbreaks.more: An ICMR-led virological analysis in New Microbes and New Infections (via a secondary summary) identifies an A/Missouri/11/2025(H1N1)pdm09-like variant within the established pdm09 lineage, not a novel reassortant. Officially, Delhi still has zero confirmed H1N1 deaths, and the government disputes media reports of fatalities. Surveillance runs through 73 ICMR labs testing severe-acute-respiratory-infection samples weekly. Dengue is rising alongside it: 311 cases year-to-date at end-August and about 695 by the first week of October. No official H1N1 count newer than 31 August was located as of late October. India's post-monsoon influenza peak (August–October) is a recognised seasonal pattern.
outbreaks.src: Delhi Health Dept data via OneIndia, 3 Sep 2026; Outlook India (ICMR DG statement), 25 Aug 2026; Business Today, 21–22 Aug 2026; The Hans India (Delhi dengue), Oct 2026; bioengineer.org summary of New Microbes and New Infections, Sep 2026

outbreaks.title: Cholera Outbreak — Myanmar
outbreaks.desc: A cholera outbreak has killed at least three people in Myanmar and hospitalized hundreds more with diarrhea — one death in Yangon, two in Sittwe (Rakhine State) — straining a health system already affected by civil war and economic disruption. A separate, smaller outbreak from the West/Central Africa cluster tracked above. ECDC counts only 272 cases in Myanmar as of 22 June 2026 (versus 1,888 at the same point in 2025), so this is a much smaller outbreak than last year's.
outbreaks.src: Bloomberg, 18 Aug 2026; ECDC Cholera Worldwide Overview

outbreaks.title: Andes Hantavirus — Cruise Ship (M/V Hondius), Multi-country
outbreaks.desc: Fifth and reportedly final DON on this cluster. Following notification 2 May of severe acute respiratory illness aboard, 13 cases confirmed/probable across passengers and crew (147 aboard), including 3 deaths (23% CFR). A probable case in Tristan da Cunha was later lab-confirmed after disembarkation.
outbreaks.more: CDC assessed overall US public risk as extremely low throughout; coordination extended to State Department travel guidance for affected Americans.
outbreaks.src: WHO DON-611, DON-599; CDC HAN-528/529

outbreaks.title: Nipah Virus — Kerala, India (June 2026)
outbreaks.status: Monitoring — single case, no secondary transmission reported
outbreaks.desc: Kerala's health department confirmed a laboratory-confirmed Nipah case in an adult male in Kozhikode district on 11 June 2026 (symptom onset 30 May; hospitalized 10 June with neurological manifestations and on ventilatory support in intensive care). As of 18 June, 104 contacts — including health and care workers — were under monitoring with no secondary cases, and as of 23 June there was still no evidence of secondary transmission. April–September is Kerala's recognised Nipah high-alert period; roughly a dozen confirmed cases have been reported in Kerala over the past five years.
outbreaks.more: Kerala has had recurrent Nipah spillover since 2018 (2019, 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025), typically single cases or small clusters contained quickly by state and central rapid-response teams. This event is separate from the January 2026 West Bengal healthcare-worker cluster tracked above.
outbreaks.src: WHO DON-609, 25 Jun 2026; npj Viruses, May 2026

outbreaks.title: Infant Formula Contaminated with Cereulide Toxin — Multi-country
outbreaks.desc: WHO reported that precautionary recalls of infant formula linked to cereulide (a heat-stable Bacillus cereus toxin) spanned 99 countries and territories, with 144 suspected and confirmed illnesses in ten countries between 1 January and 25 February 2026; Belgium is the only country with laboratory-confirmed cases (8). Investigations point to arachidonic acid (ARA) oil used as a formula ingredient as the likely source, but a complete root-cause analysis and batch traceability had not been established. WHO rated the overall public-health risk moderate; ECDC and EFSA later concluded that, because of the recalls, the current likelihood of exposure is low, with most affected infants mildly ill and some hospitalized for dehydration.
outbreaks.more: EFSA published a rapid risk assessment on 2 February 2026 deriving an acute reference dose and action levels that Belgium and others adopted for recall decisions. In July 2026 the US FDA pressed infant-formula makers to tighten supplier oversight after this event and two separate US infant-botulism outbreaks (ByHeart, Nara Organics), all traced to ingredient supply chains rather than home handling.
outbreaks.src: WHO via Food Safety Magazine, 19 Mar 2026; ECDC/EFSA rapid outbreak assessment, Feb 2026; EFSA, 2 Feb 2026; Contemporary Pediatrics (FDA letter), 13 Jul 2026

outbreaks.src: WHO DON, 14 Feb 2026

outbreaks.title: Nipah Virus — India
outbreaks.desc: In January 2026 two healthcare workers at a private hospital in Barasat (North 24 Parganas, West Bengal) were laboratory-confirmed with Nipah virus at NIV Pune. The probable index patient, a 55-year-old woman who had consumed raw date-palm sap, died. Sequencing matched Bangladesh 2022-lineage strains at 99% identity, consistent with nosocomial transmission. More than 190 contacts tested negative, aided by an NIV Pune mobile BSL-3 laboratory. WHO assesses the risk as low.
outbreaks.src: WHO DON-593 (India notification, 26 Jan 2026); npj Viruses, May 2026

outbreaks.desc: Outbreak declared over after two incubation periods (42 days) with no new cases. Final tally: 19 cases (14 confirmed, 5 probable), 14 deaths. 857 contacts completed monitoring. An earlier DON on the same outbreak was issued 21 Nov 2025.
outbreaks.src: WHO DON-592; earlier DON 21 Nov 2025

governance.title: UK Launches £100m AI Biosecurity Lab Backed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind
governance.desc: On 24 October 2026 the UK Cabinet Office announced an AI Biosecurity Lab, which the government describes as the world's first dedicated AI-biosecurity organisation. It will be an independent non-profit within a new National AI Biosecurity Initiative, with £100 million of government funding plus up to £200 million in company commitments. OpenAI is providing £100 million in compute and model credits and trusted access through its Rosalind Biodefense programme. Anthropic is providing up to £100 million in model credits, trusted model access and technical support. Google DeepMind is contributing scientists and access to Gemini and science models, and Basecamp Research its AI-biology models. Government partners are UKHSA, APHA, Dstl and the MHRA. The initial focus is early threat detection and faster vaccines and countermeasures. Significance: this is the clearest example yet of a state institutionalising 'defensive acceleration' — using frontier labs' own models for biodefence — rather than relying only on restricting access. It also creates a model India could study for pairing its One Health Mission and ICMR labs with frontier AI. Sources: Unite.AI (23–26 Oct 2026), Bloomberg (23 Oct 2026).

governance.title: UN General Assembly Adopts Pandemic Declaration by Vote After US Blocks Consensus
governance.desc: The political declaration from the second UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response (25 September 2026) could not be adopted by consensus because of US objections. It was instead adopted by a recorded vote in the General Assembly on 12 October: 153 in favour, 3 against (United States, Israel, Argentina) and 2 abstentions (New Zealand, Paraguay). The non-binding text welcomes the 2025 WHO Pandemic Agreement and calls for 'the timely completion of the PABS annex'; the US objected in part to those references to the annex negotiations. Significance: it confirms that the US is outside the WHO pandemic architecture, and it adds political pressure — but no legal force — to the stalled annex talks. Sources: AllAfrica/UN News, 13 Oct 2026; Times of Oman, Oct 2026; WHO, 18 Sep 2026.

governance.title: India Issues Minimum Standards for High-Containment Labs Under the National One Health Mission
governance.desc: The 'Minimum Standard Requirements for High-Containment Facilities Under the National One Health Mission, 2026' were released at the Mission's Scientific Steering Committee meeting on 30 September 2026 and are hosted by the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser (associated with ICMR, DBT and MoHFW). They set the conditions a BSL-3 laboratory must meet to join the Mission's high-risk-pathogen laboratory network: verified containment, equipment, access control and waste handling; trained staff, documented procedures, emergency plans and periodic safety checks; and data sharing under documented agreements that protect personal and sensitive data. Labs must first meet the existing 2024 national certification guidelines. Significance: this is India's most concrete recent step toward a networked, auditable high-containment system. It strengthens biosafety (containment and operations) but does not by itself create the biosecurity-specific law or agency that ORF flagged as missing. Source: The Policy Edge, 17 Oct 2026 (linking the PSA PDF).

governance.title: PABS Annex: IGWG8 Ends Without Consensus; IGWG9 Set for 2–13 November
governance.desc: The eighth session of the Intergovernmental Working Group (14–18 September 2026) negotiated the definitions, implementation and governance sections of the PABS annex. Delegations reported growing convergence but no consensus. The main splits, as reported by TWN, are: (1) whether 'pathogens with pandemic potential' is a closed list or an open-ended scope, with both list-based and risk-assessment approaches now in play; (2) developed countries seeking access to epidemic or PHEIC pathogens before any benefit commitments; (3) sample and sequence sharing — developed countries propose notifying WHO within 24 hours, while others want a risk assessment first ('as soon as possible' or 48 hours) and dispute whether sharing should be a legal obligation; and (4) whether the Conference of the Parties or the Director-General appoints the PABS Advisory Group. Informal drafting took place on 5–9 October; IGWG9 runs 2–13 November 2026, ahead of the WHA80 deadline in May 2027. Relevance: these sharing rules will decide how quickly sequences from outbreaks like Bundibugyo Ebola flow to countermeasure developers. Sources: WHO, 18 Sep 2026; Third World Network, 4 Oct 2026.

governance.title: CRS Update: Congress Weighs Several AI–Biosecurity Bills; Synthesis-Screening Framework Still Unrevised
governance.desc: A Congressional Research Service primer updated 15 September 2026 states that no federal law broadly regulates AI in the biological sciences and that OSTP has not revised the 2024 nucleic-acid synthesis screening framework, despite EO 14292. It lists pending bills: H.R. 3029 (Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act, passed the House); S. 3741 (Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026); S. 4363 (Engineering Biology Readiness Act); S. 4069 (AI-Ready Bio-Data Standards Act); S. 3952 (Future of Artificial Intelligence Innovation Act of 2026); and H.R. 9307 / S. 4770 (Web of Biological Data Act of 2026). It also notes NIST's warning that AI-designed sequences could evade current screening tools, and that Anthropic reported in September that some users circumvented its biosafety safeguards while describing them as 'working scientists'. Source: a secondary summary of the CRS text; individual bill status was not independently checked on Congress.gov.

governance.title: House Companion Introduced: H.R. 10197 Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (Pfluger–Houlahan)
governance.desc: Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX), with Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-PA), introduced H.R. 10197 on 31 August 2026 — a bipartisan House counterpart to the Senate's S.3741 (Cotton–Klobuchar). It would make nucleic-acid synthesis screening legally mandatory for sellers of DNA and RNA sequences and of the equipment that makes them. Sellers would have to verify customer identity, establish the purpose of each order, screen against a federal list of sequences of concern published by the Department of Commerce, and notify Commerce about high-risk buyers. Violations would carry civil penalties of up to $750,000 each, and the rules would take effect one year after enactment. Status: referred to House Energy and Commerce; no markup recorded. Significance: with companion bills now in both chambers, a mandatory-screening statute is plausible for the first time — though, as this tracker's AI-bio entries note, homology-based screening alone can be evaded by AI-redesigned sequences. Source: The Lobby News bill tracker (H.R. 10197).

governance.title: BWC Working Group: ~90% of Draft Report Agreed; Verification, Financing Unresolved Before Final December Session
governance.desc: At its ninth session (ending 21 August 2026 in Geneva), the Working Group on Strengthening the Biological Weapons Convention advanced a draft report covering seven areas: international cooperation, science and technology developments, confidence-building measures, verification, national implementation, response preparedness and institutional arrangements. It is mandated to establish, by consensus, a mechanism to review science and technology developments and another for international cooperation under Article X. BWPP reported about 90.6% of the text agreed early in the session. Still unresolved: verification, transfer controls, trust-fund financing (the US objected to language allowing contributions from non-state actors such as the EU), and three issues the Chair set aside (sanctions as a compliance tool, decision-making for new bodies, and the powers of the Meeting of States Parties). Russia and Iran raised formal objections. A final four-day session is scheduled for December 2026, and the 2027 Review Conference will decide what takes effect. The Chair cited AI–biology convergence as a driver of urgency. Source: Global Biodefense, 19 Aug 2026.

governance.title: NTI | bio Releases First Proactive Input-Screening Tool for AI Protein-Design Models
governance.desc: NTI | bio published a first-of-its-kind proof-of-concept input-screening method for AI-enabled protein-design tools — screening what goes INTO a biological AI model, rather than only screening synthesis orders on the way out. Directly responds to the finding (tracked in this tool's AI-Bio module) that open protein-design tools currently have almost no equivalent guardrails to those applied to DNA synthesis orders.

governance.title: OpenAI "Biodefense in the Intelligence Age" action plan
governance.desc: An action plan for AI-powered biological resilience, published alongside OpenAI's own biodefense summit — positions frontier labs as active participants in defensive biosecurity infrastructure, not just sources of dual-use risk.

governance.title: China's National Health Development Plan — AI-Pharma Provisions
governance.desc: China's National Health Development Plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan Period, officially released 7 Jul 2026, explicitly proposes promoting AI-enabled upgrading across the entire pharmaceutical industry value chain. Chinese regulators are concurrently building a multi-layered regulatory framework spanning data, algorithms, cybersecurity, biosafety, and healthcare regulation for this expansion.

governance.title: US Policy for Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research
governance.desc: Prohibits federally funded dangerous gain-of-function (DGOF) research and establishes new review requirements for potential DGOF research and international research of concern (IROC). Supersedes an earlier DURC/PEPP policy consolidation before it took effect. Per a 16 Jul 2026 Congressional Research Service report, this policy did NOT revise or replace the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening — the separate 90-day synthesis-screening revision mandated by EO 14292 remains, per CRS, unconfirmed as fulfilled.

governance.title: Coalition Open Letter Calls for Mandatory (Not Voluntary) Synthesis Screening
governance.desc: A coalition of life-sciences researchers, AI companies, and biotechnology developers issued an open letter calling on Congress to make synthetic nucleic acid order screening legally mandatory, placing enforceable responsibility on DNA synthesis companies rather than relying on the current voluntary/self-governance model (IGSC, IBBIS Common Mechanism).

governance.title: Anthropic Proposes Government Accountability Framework for Frontier AI
governance.desc: Anthropic released a proposed policy framework recommending that frontier AI developers test models for catastrophic risks (including biological), publish findings, and be held accountable to a government agency — a call for external, not just self-imposed, oversight of the risk categories it and OpenAI both now publish internal assessments on.

governance.title: WHO Pandemic Agreement: PABS Annex Not Agreed; Negotiations Extended to May 2027
governance.desc: WHO Member States failed to agree the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) annex to the Pandemic Agreement at the IGWG session of 27 April–1 May 2026, and agreed to extend negotiations; the annex is now expected to be resubmitted no later than the World Health Assembly in May 2027, with a further IGWG session held 6–17 July 2026. The main divide is between many developing and emerging economies (including the Africa Group and the Group for Equity) and several industrialised countries, including EU Member States. Relevance: pathogen-sample and sequence sharing rules are the mechanism the Agreement relies on for outbreaks such as Bundibugyo Ebola. Update: the July session and IGWG8 (14–18 September) also ended without consensus — see the September/October entries.

governance.title: OpenAI Publishes Governance Framework Covering CBRN Risk
governance.desc: OpenAI published a governance framework describing its risk assessment and mitigation processes across four categories: cyber offense; chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risks; harmful manipulation; and loss of control. Includes an active bounty program of up to $50,000 for researchers who find jailbreaks of ChatGPT's biosafety safeguards specifically.

governance.title: Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S.3741) introduced
governance.desc: Introduced in the US Senate; read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

governance.title: S.3741 Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act Introduced (Cotton–Klobuchar)
governance.desc: Bipartisan Senate bill that would direct the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations on nucleic-acid synthesis security, making gene-synthesis order and customer screening a mandatory, federally enforceable near-term stopgap while a broader biosecurity strategy is developed (with exemptions for clearly non-hazardous sequences). As of the early-2026 commentary reviewed, it had not advanced beyond introduction. Update: a CRS primer (15 Sep 2026) still lists S. 3741 among pending bills.

governance.title: IBBIS International Standards Initiative launched (Singapore)
governance.desc: Meeting convened stakeholders from industry, government, academia and standards bodies to push consistent global adoption of DNA synthesis screening.

governance.title: EU Biotech Act — Biosecurity & Biodefence Provisions (Pillar 7)
governance.desc: European Commission legislative proposal COM(2025) 1022, Pillar 7, amends multiple existing EU health and food regulations to boost biodefence and biosecurity and help prevent biotechnology misuse. Stakeholder consultation (14 May–11 Jun 2025) gathered 222 contributions from industry, NGOs, and public authorities.

governance.title: Russian MFA Statement on AI-Enabled Biological Risk (BWC Conference)
governance.desc: At a BWC 50th-anniversary conference held in New Delhi, Russia's Deputy Director-General for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control formally flagged that new AI models could enable researchers to design a wider range of molecules/proteins, modify microorganisms to be undetectable, and develop new bioagents and toxins — calling for export-control attention to dual-use gene-editing platforms. References Russia's own recurring Sochi biosecurity forum (Rospotrebnadzor + MFA, most recently 10–11 Jun 2025).

governance.title: Executive Order 14292
governance.desc: Directs revision or replacement of the 2024 OSTP nucleic-acid synthesis screening framework.

governance.title: OSTP Screening Framework takes effect for purchases
governance.desc: Nucleic acid synthesis screening becomes a live requirement for purchases (condition of federal life-sciences research funding).

governance.title: India's Biosecurity Governance Gap (documented, not yet acted on)
governance.desc: ORF's 'Biosecurity blueprint for India' documents that India has no dedicated biosecurity-specific law or agency — biological risk is currently governed only through general instruments (Environment Protection Act 1986, WMD Act 2005, Biosafety Rules 1989/rDNA Guidelines 2017), which address biosafety and non-proliferation but not biosecurity as a distinct function. ORF recommends a dedicated biosecurity agency, drawing on the US's NSCEB model. This gap remains undocumented as closed as of this tracker's last check — tracked here as a standing recommendation, not a completed action.

governance.title: IBBIS Common Mechanism launched
governance.desc: Free, open-source, globally available DNA/RNA synthesis screening software released.

governance.title: OSTP Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening issued
governance.desc: Established as a voluntary-turned-conditional requirement tied to federal life-sciences funding eligibility.

governance.title: IBBIS founded as independent Swiss foundation
governance.desc: Incubated out of NTI | bio; headquartered Geneva.

governance.title: HHS voluntary synthesis-screening guidance
governance.desc: Baseline (non-binding) starting point for US gene-synthesis screening policy.
